prize_parts.citation: for foundational contributions to the analysis of nominal rigidities and monetary policy: time-dependent price setting, staggered contracts and policy rules, and a microfounded framework for evaluating policy

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged after round 1: B001, credited to Taylor, Woodford and Calvo. I have only sharpened the criterion and the citation. I rank B001 first on originality, breadth, durability and demonstrated influence. Nominal rigidity is the central reason money and monetary policy have real effects. Calvo gave a tractable pricing device. Taylor gave staggered contracts and an interest-rate rule. Woodford gave an integrated, welfare-based framework for evaluating policy. Each can be tied to a specific body of work, and each was later used as a benchmark by others, including state-dependent pricing models. The chair asked what separates these three from Gali, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets. My criterion is origination of a separable, general idea on which the later literature depends. Gali and Gertler, with Clarida, codified and applied the canonical model. Christiano and Eichenbaum made it empirically usable. Smets brought it into central-bank practice. These are real contributions, but they build on the originating ideas. A different criterion, such as identified estimation or institutional adoption, would change the laureate set. It would also produce a different discovery, and I do not think that discovery is the stronger one. On the Taylor rule, I treat it as a scientific contribution because it is a simple, testable characterisation of policy behaviour and a normative benchmark, and not only a prescription. I have not independently verified this. The ideas are 25 to 45 years old and have been tested through 2008, the zero lower bound and the post-2021 inflation. The 2022 prize went to banking and financial crises, not to this core. I do not use support counts as merit. B001 is the one entry every member either prefers or lists as an alternative, but that is not a vote count. My case rests on the science. I also correct my round-1 statement that eleven of eleven opening proposals contained Calvo, Taylor and Woodford. The chair's record shows ten of eleven, because Boppart's opening used Gali in place of Calvo, and Boppart has since moved to the same trio.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is still attribution. A trio built on origin points excludes people with strong claims on the canonical model, on estimation and on adoption, and the committee could reasonably decide that the credit is too broad for three names. The second reservation comes from my own field. Evidence on price adjustment shows a mix of time and state dependence, and our own menu-cost work finds asymmetric adjustment that the Calvo device does not capture. The device is therefore a tractable benchmark, not a literal description. The framework's fit in the post-2021 inflation, and its treatment of heterogeneity, are genuinely debated. I regard these as limits on the claim, not refutations, but a prize centred on a benchmark is only as strong as the case that benchmarks count as discoveries. Earlier macro prizes (Lucas, Kydland-Prescott, Sargent-Sims) also cover adjacent ground. Finally, no entry has an explicit majority in round 1, and B001's broad acceptability as an alternative may reflect that it offends fewer members rather than that it persuades more.

responses.point: Hassler, the chair, prefers B002 (Kiyotaki and Moore) for its clean two-author attribution. He accepts that B001 has a first-order claim but regards the exclusion of Gali, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets as a larger attribution cost than anything in B002.
responses.response: I agree that B002 has the cleaner attribution, and I do not weigh clean credit as lightly as my ranking might suggest. Two things keep B001 ahead for me. First, the exclusions in B001 are of people who extended and estimated the framework, whereas Kiyotaki and Moore are the sole originators of their mechanism. The question is whether the 'derivative' label for the excluded group is fair, and I think it is for Gali and Gertler but less clearly for Christiano and Eichenbaum, whose identification work changed what could be believed. Second, B002 is partly adjacent to the 2022 prize, and you and others agree its empirical support comes mostly from calibrated or later work by others. If the committee concludes B001's credit cannot be bounded, B002 is a serious macro fallback. I do not rank it among my alternatives only because my own field gives me a better basis for B015 and B021. I also disclose that you are my co-author on the menu-costs paper, so you should discount my reading of B001's pricing foundations accordingly. I am not adjudicating that.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson prefers B006 and keeps B001 as her first alternative. She says the lack of a recent overlapping prize helps B001. She says my own admission about excluded contributors means the committee would be choosing among near-equal claims, whereas B006's credit boundary is easier to defend.
responses.response: I accept the point about the credit boundary, but I would not call the claims near-equal. They are of different kinds, and the chair's question asks the committee to say which kind it is rewarding. If the discovery is the nominal-rigidity framework, the three originating contributions are separable and the others sit downstream. If the committee prefers to reward estimation and quantification, the claims are indeed close and the trio fails. I am willing to name that as the crux, and it is the main reason I list B021 and B015 as fallbacks, where credit is cleaner. On B006 I should be candid. It is outside my field and I did not rank it in my opening, so I defer to colleagues like you and Teorell on whether the within-polity rules-to-policy programme is distinct from the 2024 prize. I can say that your suggestion to frame the citation around the framework and testable predictions seems sensible. I do not treat B006's cleaner attribution as outweighing B001's breadth, but that is a weighting judgement and I do not claim it is settled.

responses.point: Strömberg moved from B015 first to B001 and argues the award should rest on the originating ideas (pricing device, contract structure, policy-rule framework), not on how well estimated DSGE descendants forecast. He keeps B015 as an alternative and notes that only four members ranked it.
responses.response: I agree with the originating-ideas framing and I would put it in the citation, because it also answers the empirical critique. A prize for Calvo, Taylor and Woodford does not need the post-2021 record to vindicate the DSGE descendants. It needs the original ideas to have changed how the field reasons, and I think they did. I would add one qualification to your framing. The state-dependence evidence from micro price data bears on the pricing device itself, not only on the descendants, so I would word the citation around time-dependent price setting as an analytical benchmark and not as a description of firm behaviour. On B015, I agree that four rankings is thin and that it cannot be called a shared view. My own case for it rests on its role in merger review and welfare analysis. I would not add Bresnahan to a trio without a clear priority argument over Levinsohn's co-authorship of the central paper. My field proximity to IO is a reason for me to be careful on B015, not to push it.

responses.point: Krusell prefers B001 with Calvo, Taylor and Woodford. He reads the post-2021 inflation and heterogeneous-agent work as extending the framework and not discarding it, and he would not move to Gali or Gertler unless the committee wanted to reward estimation.
responses.response: I agree that the origin-point logic is the right test for this award and that moving to Gali or Gertler would change the discovery. Where I would be more cautious is the claim that the framework was extended and not discarded. That is a fair description of the heterogeneous-agent literature. My field gives a related reason for caution. The evidence on state-dependent pricing and on asymmetric adjustment shows that a benchmark can organise policy analysis while being a poor description of micro behaviour. I would not treat the inflation episode as validation, and I think the citation should avoid wording that implies it. You disclose field proximity to the successor literature, and I take that as a reason to read your assessment of how well the framework has held up with some care, as I would for my own. I do not think it changes the scientific argument for the three names.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept an originating-ideas criterion for B001, or will insist on crediting Gali, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum or Smets for the canonical, estimated and adopted model, which would change the laureate set.
Whether the Taylor rule is accepted as a scientific contribution, and how Calvo, Taylor, Fischer and Phelps priority questions are resolved. I have not independently verified these priority claims.
How much the mixed micro evidence on time versus state dependence, the post-2021 inflation episode and heterogeneity should count against a prize centred on a benchmark framework.

If B001 stalls, whether B021 (Melitz and Helpman, with a citation centred on selection and the gains from trade, not on all firm-level research) or B015 (Pakes, Berry and Levinsohn, if toolkit contributions count as discoveries) is the more defensible fallback. I would support either, but I cannot say which the committee would prefer.
No entry has an explicit majority in round 1, and I cannot infer hidden support from the member files.
statement.conflict_note: Disclosed, not adjudicated. I co-authored 'Menu Costs and Asymmetric Price Adjustment' (IJIO 2026) with the chair, John Hassler, and former chair Tore Ellingsen. The paper is adjacent to the price-setting topics in B001, and I have responded to Hassler's B002 position above. My field is industrial organization and international trade, so I have proximity to B015 and B021, both of which are my listed alternatives, not my preferred part. None of the credited names on the shortlist appears among my listed co-authors. The profile notes a public family relationship with a Swedish political leader. I record it as a public fact, and nothing in the profile suggests it bears on these scientific candidates, so I give it no weight.
